content: Linea nigra, which translates from Latin as black line, is a dark vertical line that commonly develops on the abdomen during pregnancy. It is also referred to as linea nigra. This line is a form of hyperpigmentation, which occurs due to an increased production of melanin, the pigment responsible for skin color. The hyperpigmentation is believed to be triggered by elevated levels of estrogen during pregnancy. This same hormonal mechanism is responsible for the darkening of the areolas. However, the specific reason why this pigmentation process occurs along the midline of the abdomen remains unclear. Women with fair skin are less likely to develop linea nigra compared to women with darker skin tones. Before the dark line becomes visible, it may initially appear as a lighter, less noticeable line called the linea alba, or white line. Linea nigra typically becomes noticeable during the second trimester of pregnancy. Some studies have suggested a potential association between the development of linea nigra and insulin levels, although this link requires further investigation. The most prominent sign of linea nigra is a brownish streak, usually about one centimeter in width. This line runs vertically along the midline of the abdomen, extending from the pubic area to the xiphoid process, which is the lowermost part of the rib cage located at the tip of the sternum. No medical treatment is necessary for linea nigra, as it is a benign and natural occurrence during pregnancy. Some anecdotal evidence suggests that dietary supplementation with folic acid may help reduce the intensity of the discoloration. After childbirth, the line typically fades gradually over time, although it may not disappear completely in some cases.
